hypotheses.statement: Compared to negative or neutral mood, positive mood leads to asymmetric, self-serving responses to ambiguous social comparison targets (assimilation to upward, contrast from downward).
Self-serving asymmetric responding requires ambiguous similarity information; in its absence responses are symmetric.
Negative mood is associated with symmetric, objective (non-self-serving) responding.
Self-serving reinterpretation under positive mood is effortful and is disrupted by cognitive load.

computed.stated_design: 2(direction) x 2(cue) factorial, all participants received the positive mood manipulation
computed.derivation: For a 2-group comparison, residual df cannot exceed N-2 under ANY convention (recomputed on the subset, or reusing the omnibus's pooled error df=43). Female university (N = 47) students participated is explicitly stated; the omnibus manipulation-check and self-evaluation tests in the same experiment (F(1,43)=38.80; F(1,43)=7.77; F(1,43)=5.99) all confirm a 4-cell/N=47/df2=43 model. The 'unshared birthday' simple effect, drawn from only 2 of those 4 cells (a strict subset of the 47 participants, since shared-birthday-condition results are also reported), cannot have MORE residual degrees of freedom (46) than the absolute ceiling for any 2-group test on the full N=47 sample (45), let alone more than the omnibus's own df2=43.

findings.notes: This is a cross-reference contradiction between two df values printed in the same paragraph/section of the same paper, not an assumed external bound -- N=47 and the 4-cell design (df2=43) are both explicitly stated. Rated highly_suspicious rather than impossible because it rests on the standard ANOVA residual-df formula (df2 = n - cells), which the paper does not state explicitly, though it is the only convention consistent with every OTHER df in Experiment 1. An innocent explanation is a typo (e.g. df2=46 for an intended 26, or a copy-paste from an unrelated analysis).

computed.positive_mood_subset_design: 2(cue) x 2(direction), 4 cells, within positive mood only
computed.derivation: The omnibus 3-way ANOVA (mood x direction x cue) on the factorial-only data (excluding the separately-reported no-mood control) reports df2=118 for an 8-cell model, implying total factorial N=126 (118+8). The positive-mood-only 2x2 subset ANOVA reports df2=124 for a 4-cell model (124+4=128). Since n_positive + n_negative = 126 and both moods have participants (negative-mood results are also reported, so n_negative>0), n_positive must be STRICTLY LESS than 126, and in fact at most 122 given df2=124 requires n_positive>=128 alone -- exceeding the total factorial pool by at least 2, and exceeding the loosest theoretical ceiling (122, if n_negative approached 0) by 2 as well. The parallel negative-mood-only subset (F(1,124)=56.97 for direction) implies the identical n_negative=128 under the same logic.

findings.notes: Same class of finding as exp1_df_impossible_subset: two df values printed within the same section of the same paper (118 for the 8-cell omnibus, 124 for both 4-cell mood subsets) are mutually inconsistent under the standard ANOVA residual-df formula. Capped at highly_suspicious rather than impossible for the same reason -- reliance on the unstated but standard df=n-cells convention -- and because a subset-ANOVA using a separately-recomputed (not pooled) error term is one of several plausible reporting conventions this paper does not specify.

findings.quote: Those in the negative mood (M = 6.98, SD = .53), positive mood (M = 6.98, SD = .80), and the control condition (M = 6.82, SD = .67), did not differ F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76.
findings.notes: The three-group (negative/positive/control) mood-ANOVA one sentence earlier is correctly reported as F(2, 42) = 18.44 -- df1=2, matching the 3 groups. The self-evaluations ANOVA on the SAME 3 groups is printed with df1=1, which is the wrong numerator df for a 3-group one-way ANOVA and does not reproduce the printed p=.76 (computed p=.606 at df1=1, outside the achievable interval). Recomputed at the correct df1=2 for 3 groups, F=.27 gives p=.765, which matches the printed p=.76 exactly. This reads as a transcription/typo error (df1 printed as 1 instead of 2) rather than a fabricated statistic, but it is a genuine, verifiable inconsistency in a load-bearing sentence (the paper's own justification that the mood manipulations, alone, did not affect self-evaluations).

Both readings are non-significant so no decision is reversed, but the magnitude gap (.224 vs .83, roughly 3.7x) is unexplained by rounding or tail convention.
